title: Why did the first cities and states begin?
essentialQuestion: How did larger settlements change work, rules, cooperation and power?
learningGoal: Explain how surplus food, special jobs, rulers, laws, taxes and writing helped the first cities and states work, and who gained power.

warmUp.question: When thousands of people live in one place, what do they need to share?

evidence.label: Fictional example created for this lesson.
evidence.question: Which changes in Banwa need people to work together? Which changes could give some people more power?

events.text: Farms near Banwa grow extra grain for several good years.
People build a shared storehouse and guard it.
Potters, builders, traders and record keepers each do one main job.
Leaders organise a canal and make rules about who can use the water.
Some families control more land and grain than others.

sections.heading: Extra food helped the first cities grow
sections.text: More than 5,000 years ago, some farming towns grew into the first cities. One of the earliest was Uruk, in Mesopotamia, in what is now Iraq. Other early cities grew beside the Nile in Egypt and the Indus River in South Asia. Some grew in the Yellow River valley in China. Later, cities also grew in Mexico, Central America and West Africa. Every city needed a food surplus. With extra food, thousands of people could eat without farming. Then many people could specialise in one kind of work. They became builders, potters, traders or priests. In Banwa, extra grain lets potters, builders and record keepers each do one main job.
sections.simpler: More than 5,000 years ago, the first cities began. Uruk, in what is now Iraq, was one of the first. Other cities grew by big rivers in Egypt, South Asia and China. Later, cities grew in the Americas and West Africa. A city needs a surplus, or extra food. Then many people do not need to farm. They can specialise. Some build, and some trade. In Banwa, extra grain lets people do one main job.

sections.heading: States had rulers, laws and taxes
sections.text: Many cities became part of a state. A state is a group of people in one area who are led by one government. Rulers and officials made choices for everyone and settled arguments. They also made laws, which are rules that everyone must follow. In Babylon, King Hammurabi had about 280 laws carved on a tall black stone. States collected taxes too, and people often paid in grain, animals or work. In Egypt, farmers gave part of their harvest to the ruler. Taxes paid for canals, walls, storehouses and temples. In Banwa, leaders organise a canal and make rules about the water.
sections.simpler: Many cities became part of a state. A state is an area with one government. Its leaders make laws. A law is a rule that all people must follow. In Babylon, King Hammurabi put his laws on a big stone. People also paid a tax, often in grain or work. The tax paid for walls and canals. In Banwa, the leaders plan a canal and make water rules.

sections.heading: Writing helped, but power was not shared equally
sections.text: To collect taxes and share out food, officials needed to keep track of a lot. So some early states began to keep a record in writing. In Mesopotamia, people pressed marks into wet clay to count grain and animals. Egypt, China and the Maya of Central America also made their own writing. The Indus cities had signs too, but nobody can read them yet. Working together, a city could build things that one family could not. But power was not shared equally. Rulers, officials and rich families often controlled land, grain and water. Some laws protected people, but others helped the powerful more.
sections.simpler: Leaders needed to count lots of grain. So some states started to keep a record in writing. In what is now Iraq, people pressed marks into wet clay to count grain. Egypt, China and the Maya made writing too. No one can read the Indus signs yet. In a city, people can build big things together. But power is not shared fairly. Rulers and rich families often have more land and grain. Some laws help the rich more.

glossary.definition: More food or goods than people need right now.
glossary.example: Banwa's surplus grain fed the potters, builders and record keepers.

glossary.definition: To do mostly one kind of work and get good at it.
glossary.example: In Banwa, some people specialise as builders or record keepers.

glossary.definition: A group of people in one area, led by one government.
glossary.example: Ancient Egypt was a state with a ruler, officials and laws.

glossary.definition: A rule that everyone in a place must follow.
glossary.example: King Hammurabi's laws were carved on a tall black stone.

glossary.definition: Money, goods or work that people must give to their government.
glossary.example: In Banwa, two baskets of grain were given to the leaders as tax.

glossary.definition: Written information that is kept so people can check it later.
glossary.example: The Banwa record keeper wrote down how much grain each farm brought.

checks.question: Why did early cities need a food surplus?

options.text: So that nobody in the city had to work
options.feedback: Not quite. City people worked hard, but at jobs other than farming. Look again at the first part.

options.text: So that many people could do other jobs
options.feedback: Yes. Extra food fed builders, potters, traders and priests, so they did not need to grow food.

options.text: So the city would not need any trade at all
options.feedback: Not quite. Cities had traders, and trade was one of the special jobs. Look again at the first part.

checks.question: Why did some early states begin to use writing?

options.text: To keep track of grain, animals and taxes
options.feedback: Yes. The first writing, in what is now Iraq, counted grain and animals. This helped leaders collect taxes.

options.text: To write down stories for young children
options.feedback: Not quite. The reading says the first writing was used to count things. Look at the last part.

options.text: To draw maps for traders who sailed far away
options.feedback: Not quite. The reading says the first writing was used to count things. Look at the last part.

checks.question: Can a rule help people and still be unfair? Think about the water rules in Banwa.

write.prompt: Explain how Banwa changed as it grew. Use at least three steps from the evidence and say who gained more power.
sentenceStarters: Some people gained more power because ...
selfCheck: I used at least three steps from Banwa.
I explained how one step led to the next.
I said who gained more power.
write.example: Banwa began to change when its farms grew extra grain for several years. This meant that people could build a big store for the grain. Some people could stop farming and work as potters, builders or traders. Next, the leaders planned a canal and made rules about the water. Records helped because the record keeper could count the grain and the tax. Some people gained more power because they had more land and grain than other families.

speak.partnerTask: Pick the change in Banwa you think matters most and tell your partner why. Your partner explains how it links to another change.
speak.independentTask: Say one thing a city can do because people work together, and one way a city can be unfair.

watch.title: Ancient Egypt and the Nile: A History
watch.why: The video looks closely at one real example, ancient Egypt, where a river, farming, rulers and records worked together.
watch.beforeQuestion: Watch for how the Nile River helped farming, work and the power of rulers.
watch.afterQuestion: What did people in Egypt do together? Who had more power?
watch.summary: This video tells the story of ancient Egypt, one of the world's early states. The Nile River runs through a dry desert. Each year, the river flooded and left rich soil on its banks. Farmers used this soil to grow large amounts of grain. The surplus fed many people who did other work, such as builders, craftspeople and scribes, who wrote records. The Nile was also like a road. Boats carried food, stone and other goods up and down the river. Egypt was ruled by kings called pharaohs, with many officials to help them. They collected taxes, planned work and kept records. This let Egypt build huge projects. But power was not shared equally. Egypt is only one example. Other early cities and states grew in different ways.
keyPoints: The Nile gave Egypt water, rich soil and an easy way to travel.
A food surplus let many people do special jobs.
Rulers and officials organised work and taxes, and they held most of the power.

visual.description: A world map marking six early cities, each with a small dot, its name and the modern country in brackets: Uruk (Iraq), Memphis (Egypt), Mohenjo-daro (Pakistan), Anyang (China), Tikal (Guatemala) and Jenne-jeno (Mali). The rivers beside them are drawn in blue and labelled: Tigris and Euphrates, Nile, Indus, Yellow River and Niger. No dates, so the map does not suggest a race to be first. Caption: 'Early cities grew in many parts of the world, often near rivers.'

educatorNotes: Banwa is fictional. The storehouse record shows how writing and taxes connect; you could act it out with beans or counters, with one learner as the record keeper.

Present large states as one way of organising people, not as more 'civilised' or better. The Indus cities, for example, show no clear palaces or kings, and many smaller societies had their own laws, trade and knowledge.
The video is one case study (Egypt). Remind learners that other early states grew in different ways. Lesson 12 looks at how modern cities grow; keep the two lessons separate.
changes: Lightly edited the title from 'Why did cities and states emerge?' to 'Why did the first cities and states begin?' because 'emerge' is hard for early English learners and the new title keeps it distinct from Lesson 12.
Rewrote the reading at about grade 5–6 (Base44 was about grade 10–11), cut it from four sections to three, and wrote a new simpler English version from scratch.
Added real examples from Mesopotamia, Egypt, the Indus Valley, China, Mesoamerica and West Africa, including Hammurabi's laws, grain taxes and the first writing on clay.
Kept the five Banwa steps as a timeline card and added a fictional storehouse record to link surplus, tax and writing.

New glossary (surplus, specialise, state, law, tax, record); every word appears in both the text and the simpler text. Dropped 'institution' and 'authority', which were hard to use in simpler English.
Added a warm-up, visual plan and three-item self-check; rewrote the checks so the correct answers sit in different positions.
Rewrote the video questions, summary and key points at a lower reading level; added Met Museum, OER Project (Indus) and Louvre sources alongside the Base44 OER Project link.
